newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel may widen exchange rate band.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel may widen exchange rate band.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said in an interview published in the daily newspaper Haaretz on Tuesday that the government may widen the exchange rate band from the current seven percent.
"We need, together with the Treasury, to evaluate whether the band of seven percent on each side (of the exchange rate mid-point) is enough or not. We cannot reduce it," Frenkel said.

He indicated that widening the band -- which now allows the Israeli shekel to trade seven percent above or below a sliding mid-point based on an official basket of currencies -- was part of a series of exchange rate reforms the bank was discussing with the Treasury.
Frenkel did not provide any details of the proposed changes or say when they would be completed. But he did say the reform would be "very significant".
"It will certainly create the potential for higher levels of capital movements than we see today," Frenkel said.

The Treasury and central bank have been holding talks for some time on foreign currency reform. Sources say the thrust of the proposed changes will be to raise ceilings on investment abroad by Israeli companies and financial institutions.
Frenkel defended the Bank of Israel's exchange rate policy, which has been widely criticised for creating an overvalued shekel and hurting export profitability.
Critics say that over the last 18 months the basket rate has traded at the lower end or often at the bottom of the band. As of Tuesday, the basket rate was 5.4 percent under the mid-point.
Frenkel took a longer-term view. He said that in the five years since the sliding band was instituted, the dollar and basket rates had both risen more than 42 percent.
"When you discount the increases in inflation in Israel and abroad during that period, it is clear that the appreciation in the shekel was nearly nil," Frenkel said.
